title: How Python reads your code
learningGoals: explain that Python runs lines in order, top to bottom
see that indentation is part of the code
write a first if and else with a correct indent

youtube.title: How Python Reads Your Code: Lines and Indentation | Python Programming EP 03
youtube.description: Learn why Python cares about spaces at the start of a line, with Xecxec. 0:00 Intro · 0:20 Top to bottom · 0:55 Indentation · 1:35 The two rooms · 2:05 Follow the path · 2:45 Run it · 3:05 Recap · 3:40 Bug of the Day · 4:28 Challenge · 4:48 Next episode

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today we learn why Python cares about spaces at the start of a line. In many languages they are decoration. In Python, they are part of the code.

scenes.onScreen: "Top to bottom": three numbered lines and a family-tree analogy card
scenes.animation: Lines spring in with a pop; the family-tree card slides in with parents and indented children
scenes.narration: Python reads from top to bottom. When a line ends with a colon, the lines below it, moved four spaces to the right, belong to it. Like a family tree: the children are drawn indented under their parent. Four spaces is the standard. Your editor adds them when you press the tab key.

scenes.onScreen: age.py: a decision with an indented line; faint guide lines show the indent
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 1] First a name, age, holding seventeen. [HL 2] This line asks a question: is age greater than or equal to eighteen? It ends with a colon. [HL 3] This line is moved four spaces to the right. That says, I belong to the if. It only runs if the answer is yes.

scenes.onScreen: Two coloured rooms: the if room and the else room; a door arrow between them
scenes.animation: Two rooms pop in side by side; a yes-arrow lights the if room and a no-arrow lights the else room; only one room glows at a time
scenes.narration: Think of two rooms. The if room runs when the answer is yes. The else room runs when it is no. Only one room is entered. After that, we step back out to the left, and the program carries on. Just remember: the colon opens a room, and the indent shows who lives inside.

scenes.onScreen: age.py again with the path highlighted and the output panel on the right
scenes.animation: Same code; the output panel fills line by line with a ding per output line; [TRACK] cards update
scenes.narration: [TRACK age=17] [HL 2] Seventeen is not greater than or equal to eighteen. So the answer is no. [HL 4] Python skips the if room and goes to else. [HL 5] Not yet appears. [HL 6] This last line is not indented, so it is outside both rooms, and it always runs. Done. Before we run it, predict the output with age twenty. The first line says, you can vote.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the command types with key-tick, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Run it. Not yet. Done. Change age to twenty and run again. Now you see, you can vote, and then, done.

scenes.onScreen: Recap: four ideas on one card
scenes.animation: Four recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Recap. One: Python reads top to bottom. Two: a colon opens a room, and the lines moved four spaces to the right live inside it. Three: only one of if and else runs, and then Python steps back out. Four: if the indent is wrong, you get an indentation error. Say these four ideas out loud. That is a lot already. Well done.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: else indented two spaces
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the Python error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We put else two spaces in, instead of lining it up with if. Python says, indentation error, unindent does not match any outer indentation level. The fix: line else up exactly under if.

scenes.onScreen: Python programmers are never lost. They just have a bad indent of direction.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: Python programmers are never lost. They just have a bad indent of direction.

scenes.onScreen: Task card: Eligible or Too young; test with 16, 18 and 20
scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge: change the program so it prints Eligible for age eighteen or more, and Too young otherwise. Test it with sixteen, eighteen and twenty.

scenes.onScreen: Next: EP 04 · Comments and reading a traceback
scenes.animation: Next-episode card slides up with a whoosh; right side stays empty for end-screen elements; sign-off text types in
scenes.narration: Next: comments, and how to read an error message. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.error:
Python output (exactly as Python prints it):

  File "age.py", line 4
    else:
         ^
IndentationError: unindent does not match any outer indentation level
bug.why: Python uses indentation to decide which lines belong together, so else must line up exactly under its if.

pun: "Python programmers are never lost. They just have a bad indent of direction."
challenge: Change the program so it prints Eligible for age 18 or more and Too young otherwise. Test with 16, 18 and 20.
challengeAnswer: Use if age >= 18 with print Eligible, and else with print Too young; 16 gives Too young, 18 and 20 give Eligible.

shorts.title: Spaces are code
shorts.script: In Python, spaces matter. Python uses the spaces at the start of a line, called indentation, to know which lines belong together. A line that ends with a colon opens a room. The lines moved four spaces to the right live inside that room. Four spaces is the standard. Your editor adds them when you press the tab key. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Indentation in 30 seconds.

shorts.title: The two rooms
shorts.script: If room, else room. Think of two rooms side by side. The colon opens a room, and the indent shows who lives inside. The if room runs when the answer is yes. The else room runs when the answer is no. Only one room runs, and then Python steps back out to the left and carries on. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Two rooms, one runs.

shorts.title: Follow the path
shorts.script: Which line prints? Age is seventeen, and the question asks, is age eighteen or more? The answer is no, so Python skips the if room and goes to else. Not yet appears. The last line is not indented, so it sits outside both rooms, and it always runs. Trace the path with your finger on the screen, line by line. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Trace the path.

shorts.title: IndentationError
shorts.script: Two spaces too few. Put else in the wrong place, and Python says, indentation error, unindent does not match any outer indentation level. The rule is simple. The word else must line up exactly under its if. Same column, no more, no less. Fix the spaces, and the error disappears. Your editor can show you faint guide lines to help. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Line them up.

shorts.title: Pun and challenge
shorts.script: A bad indent of direction. Python programmers are never lost, they just have one. Now your challenge. Change the program so it prints Eligible when age is eighteen or more, and Too young otherwise. Test it with sixteen, eighteen and twenty. Which ages print Eligible? Write your answer in the comments, and show us your code. Keep coding, says Xecxec! Full video: EP 03.
shorts.caption: Try it.
